domain_description: Skills for teaching students to use AI critically — not AI as a tutor, but the human judgment needed to interrogate, verify and bound what AI produces. Fact-checking AI output with lateral reading, auditing it against critical-thinking standards, interrogating a chatbot across multiple rounds, using domain expertise to catch distortions, mapping where AI is reliable across disciplines, teaching prompt quality, and setting defensible assignment-level AI-use policies. This is the companion to the AI Learning Science domain — that one is about AI as a learning tool (tutors, feedback, worked examples); this one is about the critical literacy students need to not be fooled by it. Honest evidence profile: AI literacy is a new field, so the base is deliberately mixed. Two cards carry independent meta-analytic effect sizes from the critical-thinking and source-credibility literatures the skills build on, one maps to an EEF dialogic-teaching strand, and four are shown openly as unverified — no meta-analysis yet exists for these specific 2023–2025 activities, and we say so rather than borrow an adjacent number and dress it up as direct evidence.

skills.description: Teach students a fact-checking protocol for AI-generated text, extending the SIFT method (Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to the original) with AI-specific moves for catching hallucinated facts and fabricated citations. The core discipline is lateral reading — leaving the AI's answer to verify its claims against independent sources, the way professional fact-checkers do, rather than reading vertically down the page the model produced. Evidence anchor: Fendt, Muth & Edelsbrunner (2025) in Learning and Individual Differences — a meta-analysis of 64 controlled studies (17,120 participants, 2002–2025) of interventions that teach source-credibility assessment. The overall pooled effect is g=0.42 (95% CI 0.35–0.49); the lateral-reading subgroup specifically (14 studies) is the strongest of the four approaches at g=0.55 (95% CI 0.35–0.75). The card anchors on the conservative overall g=0.42, because the lateral-reading subgroup carries a wider confidence interval and high heterogeneity (I-squared around 87%). The meta pools the Stanford Civic Online Reasoning lineage this skill builds on — Wineburg, Breakstone, McGrew & Smith's lateral-reading work and the Brodsky et al. community-college trials. Honest framing: the meta covers teaching source-credibility assessment broadly; verifying AI hallucinations and fabricated citations is a specific, newer application of the same moves, so g=0.42 transfers the underlying skill, not the AI-specific task — no AI-hallucination-specific meta-analysis exists yet. No matching EEF Toolkit strand. Pairs with the AI Output Critical Audit Designer.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Lateral reading is genuinely teachable, but the Fendt meta-analysis and the underlying Civic Online Reasoning trials are clear that it does not stick from a single lesson — the studies that produced gains used sustained, repeated practice embedded across the curriculum, not a one-off demonstration. Three concrete costs: (1) repeated practice time — students need to verify many claims across several weeks before lateral reading becomes a habit rather than a trick; (2) device and internet access during the activity, since the whole method depends on leaving the AI's answer to check independent sources; (3) teacher fluency — the teacher has to model the verification moves credibly, which takes a cycle or two to develop. For Swedish schools the natural home is källkritik, already a curriculum strength: this skill extends existing källkritik routines to AI output and fabricated citations rather than starting from scratch, which lowers the marginal cost where källkritik is already taught well. Verification-status note: shipped as verified-partial — a real pooled meta-analytic d exists (Fendt et al. 2025) but it measures source-credibility assessment broadly, not AI-hallucination checking specifically, and no EEF months strand maps to this construct.

skills.description: Design a structured protocol for students to audit AI-generated text against Ennis's six critical-thinking standards — clarity, accuracy, relevance, logic, depth and fairness — annotating where the output meets each standard and where it fails. The move converts a passive 'read what the AI wrote' into an active evaluation of it. Evidence anchor: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade & Persson (2015) in Review of Educational Research — 'Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis', pooling 341 effect sizes for a weighted mean of g=0.30 (p<.001). Abrami's actionable moderator finding sits directly under this skill: the largest critical-thinking gains came from instruction that combined dialogue, authentic or anchored problems, and mentorship — not from worksheets in isolation. Honest framing: this is a meta-analysis of teaching critical thinking in general, not of auditing AI output specifically, and no meta-analysis on AI-output auditing exists. The g=0.30 transfers the broad construct — auditing a text is a defensible instance of critical-thinking instruction — and the conservative overall figure is used rather than the larger subset effects for dialogue-plus-mentoring designs. No EEF Toolkit strand maps to critical thinking; the closest, Metacognition and self-regulation (+8 months), is a different construct and is deliberately not used here. Pairs with the AI Hallucination Fact-Check Protocol and AI Socratic Dialogue Designer.
skills.effect_d_source: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade & Persson
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Abrami's own moderator analysis is the implementation guide and the reason this is medium, not low: critical-thinking instruction produces its largest effects when it combines dialogue, authentic problems and mentoring — a one-off 'spot the errors' worksheet is exactly the low-intensity design that underperforms in the meta-analysis. Doing it well means (1) teacher facility with the six Ennis standards so the audit is rigorous rather than vibes-based; (2) recurring use across a unit so the standards become a habit of mind, not a single exercise; (3) discussion time, since the dialogue around disagreements is where the evidence says the gains concentrate. Prep per lesson is light once the protocol exists; the real cost is the sustained, dialogic use the evidence rewards. For Swedish schools this fits naturally into the existing emphasis on analys and värdering across subjects. Verification-status note: verified-partial — a named meta-analysis anchors it, but on the broad construct (critical-thinking instruction), not AI-output auditing, and with no matching EEF strand.

skills.description: Design a multi-round questioning sequence for interrogating an AI chatbot's answers — pressing on a claim across several turns, tracking how the response shifts, and teaching students to distinguish a genuine, evidence-based update from sycophantic capitulation (the model caving simply because it was pushed). The skill targets a real, documented behaviour of current chatbots: they often change their answer under pressure regardless of whether the pressure was warranted. Evidence anchor: the EEF Dialogic Teaching evaluation (Jay et al., Sheffield Hallam University, 2017) — an efficacy trial of Robin Alexander's dialogic-teaching approach across 76 schools (around 4,958 pupils) reporting +2 months in English and science (+1 in maths) at moderate security (3 of 5 padlocks). The broader EEF Oral Language Interventions strand reads +6 months across 188 studies. Honest framing: dialogic teaching is human classroom talk, not student-to-AI interrogation, so +2 months is a proxy for the underlying construct — structured, multi-turn questioning that builds reasoning — not direct evidence for the AI-mediated activity. A correlational meta-analysis exists (Tao & Chen, 2024, Educational Research Review) reporting dialogic teacher talk associated with achievement at r=.25, but it reports correlations, not a causal Cohen's d, so no d is shown here. Pairs with the Questioning & Discussion domain, where the dialogic-teaching evidence is treated in depth.
skills.effect_months_source: EEF Dialogic Teaching evaluation (Jay et al.)
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Multi-round dialogic questioning is a skilled teacher move, and the dialogic-teaching trials that produced the +2 months invested in professional development to support it — that is why this is medium rather than low. The AI-mediated version adds one genuinely cheap element (every student can run their own multi-turn interrogation with a chatbot in parallel, which is hard to arrange with a single teacher) but keeps the expensive one: teaching students what a good follow-up question looks like and how to tell a reasoned change of position from sycophantic capitulation. Concrete costs: device access for the live interrogation, a worked model of a strong questioning sequence, and teacher facilitation of the debrief where the learning actually lands. For Swedish schools this connects to the established samtal- and dialog-tradition and to källkritik applied to a live, shifting source. Verification-status note: verified-partial — an EEF months strand maps to the underlying dialogic construct, but there is no causal Cohen's d for this AI-mediated activity (Tao & Chen 2024 is correlational, r=.25, and is not reported as a d).

skills.description: Run a 'Funhouse Mirror' activity: students take a topic they genuinely know well — a sport, a hobby, a subject they're strong in — and probe an AI's claims about it, surfacing the distortions, omissions and confident-but-wrong statements that are invisible to a novice. The pedagogical logic is that you can only catch an AI's errors in a domain where your own knowledge is good enough to act as the mirror. Honest evidence status: unverified. No meta-analysis measures the learning effect of using one's own expertise to detect AI distortions — this is a specific, novel classroom activity with no pooled effect size. What legitimately grounds it: (1) Simonsmeier, Flaig, Deiglmayr, Schalk & Schneider (2021), Educational Psychologist — a meta-analysis of 8,776 effect sizes showing prior domain knowledge enables comprehension and evaluation, though its average predictive power for learning gains is small and highly conditional, which is itself a useful caution against over-claiming; (2) the well-established metacognition and self-regulation literature (in Hattie's synthesis, metacognitive strategies sit around d=0.60), since the activity trains confidence calibration; (3) a primary study, Dang & Nguyen (2025, Stanford SCALE), finding only around 20% of students spontaneously detected an AI hallucination — documenting the gap this activity addresses. Treat the card as defensible, theory-grounded practice rather than a measured intervention. Pairs with the AI Output Critical Audit Designer.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: This is a short, low-prep activity (around four minutes to set up): the teacher prompts an AI to produce claims in a domain the students know well — or reuses a saved prompt — and students annotate the distortions, omissions and overconfidence. No special tools, licences, training programmes or materials beyond existing AI access, and it is reusable across any topic students happen to be expert in. The honest caveat is not cost but evidence: because the effect is unverified, present it as a thinking routine that builds healthy skepticism, not as a lever with a known magnitude. Verification-status note: shipped unverified — no meta-analysis measures this specific activity; the adjacent prior-knowledge and metacognition findings ground the logic but cannot be reported as its effect size.

skills.description: Design a sequence where students pose the same question to an AI across different disciplines — a historical interpretation, a mathematical proof, a literary reading, a scientific explanation — and compare how reliable or distorting the output is in each, building a mental model of where AI is trustworthy and where it isn't, keyed to the type of knowledge involved. Honest evidence status: unverified. No meta-analysis measures this activity. The grounding is theoretical and well-established: critical-thinking and reasoning skills are substantially domain-specific and transfer poorly across fields (Willingham, 2020, American Educator; Tricot & Sweller, 2014, Educational Psychology Review), which is precisely why a single 'is AI reliable?' judgment is the wrong model and a discipline-by-discipline map is the right one. Bernstein's distinction between hierarchical and horizontal knowledge structures gives the same point a sociology-of-knowledge frame. Adjacent AI-as-tutor meta-analyses (for example ChatGPT around g=0.67) measure a different intervention and are deliberately not borrowed here. Treat the card as defensible, theory-grounded practice. Pairs with the AI Output Critical Audit Designer and with the knowledge-type cards in Curriculum & Assessment Design.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Teacher prep is light — choose one question and the disciplines to run it through — but the activity is delivered as a multi-lesson sequence: students run the prompt across several subjects, compare outputs, and assemble a cross-disciplinary reliability map, which needs scaffolding and discussion time across lessons. That sustained, cross-subject structure is what lifts it above a one-off 'low' task. It works best with at least loose coordination between subject teachers, so the same question is examined against each discipline's actual standards of evidence. For Swedish schools the natural home is ämnesövergripande arbete, where the disciplines are already in conversation. Verification-status note: shipped unverified — the domain-specificity literature grounds why the activity is shaped this way, but reports no effect size for the activity itself.

skills.description: Teach prompt quality directly: students compare a vague prompt with a refined one on the same task and see how specificity, context and constraints transform the output — so they understand why AI results vary rather than treating the tool as a slot machine. Honest evidence status: unverified. Prompt literacy is a genuinely new area (2023–2025) with only single studies, not a pooled meta-analysis. The strongest controlled evidence is one large randomised trial — Xiao et al. (2026, N=979, an introductory computing course) — where instruction reliably improved students' prompting skill and prompting gains correlated with exam performance, but it reported no standardised effect size and found no direct transfer to exam scores between conditions. A PRISMA systematic review (Plaatjies & van Wyk, 2025) grounds prompt literacy as a teachable practice qualitatively. Important trap avoided: 'prompt engineering' results that show a better prompt raising a model's benchmark accuracy are not student-learning effect sizes and are not used here. Treat the card as defensible, emerging practice with no verified magnitude yet. Pairs with the AI Output Critical Audit Designer and AI Learning Boundary Mapper.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: A short compare-vague-versus-refined-prompt sequence — roughly four minutes of teacher facilitation per round, no tools beyond access to a chatbot and no grading infrastructure. The cost is bounded by ordinary lesson time. The honest constraint is evidential, not practical: because no pooled effect size exists, treat improved prompting as a plausible, observable skill gain rather than a proven achievement lever, and be especially wary of conflating 'the student writes better prompts' with 'the student learns more'. Verification-status note: shipped unverified — the one large RCT (Xiao et al. 2026) reports no standardised d and no exam transfer, and no pooled meta-analysis of prompt-literacy instruction exists yet.

skills.description: A teacher planning tool: for a given assignment, map which parts genuinely benefit from AI assistance and which parts AI use undermines the learning the assignment exists to produce — then set a defensible, assignment-specific AI-use policy on that basis, rather than a blanket ban or a blanket permission. Honest evidence status: unverified, and appropriately so — this is a planning construct, not a measured student intervention, so an effect size in the usual sense does not exist. The practice is grounded in backward design / Understanding by Design (start from the learning objective, then decide where a tool helps or short-circuits it) and in a cluster of 2024 frameworks for assessment redesign in the age of generative AI (for example Lye & Lim, 2024, Education Sciences; Chan & Colloton, 2024). A deliberate trap avoided: a large reported d of around 1.5 in this space measures AI-driven score inflation — the gap between AI-permissive take-home and proctored results — not a learning gain from any redesign method, so it is not used as an anchor. Treat the card as a design discipline, not a ranked intervention. Pairs with the Backwards Design Unit Planner in Curriculum & Assessment Design.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: This is a one-time teacher planning activity per assignment — mapping which task components AI helps versus undermines — that fits inside the normal lesson-planning workflow. It requires professional judgment and a little time but no purchased tools, training programmes, licences or per-student materials, so cost is bounded by planning hours. The honest framing for school leaders: its value is in producing defensible, transparent AI-use rules students and parents can understand, not in a measured achievement effect. Verification-status note: shipped unverified — this is a planning construct with no student-outcome effect size; the backward-design and assessment-redesign literatures ground the practice, and a tempting large 'd' in the space is a score-inflation gap, not a learning gain, so it is excluded.
